title: Low Vitamin C Levels Linked to Smaller, Less Connected Brains in New Study — And South Asian Diets May Offer an Edge
excerpt: Japanese researchers scanned 2,000 brains and found that higher vitamin C in the blood correlated with more grey matter and stronger neural networks.
body:
There is a small, tart berry that has sat at the centre of Ayurvedic medicine for centuries. Amla — Indian gooseberry — contains roughly 20 times more vitamin C per gram than an orange. Your grandmother probably told you it was good for you. A new study from Japan suggests she may have been more right than she knew, and about more than just colds.

The Study

Researchers at Hirosaki University's Graduate School of Medicine measured vitamin C levels in the blood plasma of more than 2,000 adults aged 64 and older, then compared those levels against detailed MRI scans of their brains. The results, published June 10 in the journal PLOS ONE, reveal a clear pattern.

Participants with lower vitamin C levels had less grey matter volume — the brain tissue responsible for processing information, storing memories, and controlling movement. They also showed weaker connectivity within the default mode network, a constellation of brain regions that underpins attention, self-reflection, and autobiographical memory. It's the network that lets you remember your daughter's wedding or navigate a familiar route home.

"This finding generates the exciting hypothesis that a diet rich in vitamin C might play a supportive role in maintaining brain health and mitigating age-related cognitive decline in older adults," said study coauthor Tomohiro Shintaku.

The associations held even after the researchers adjusted for age, physical activity, education level, and other factors known to affect brain health.

What Vitamin C Does in the Brain

Vitamin C is not merely an immune booster. In the brain, it serves as a powerful antioxidant, neutralising free radicals that damage neurons over time. It also plays a critical role in synthesising neurotransmitters — including dopamine and norepinephrine — and in maintaining the myelin sheath that insulates nerve fibres and speeds up signal transmission.

The brain is one of the most metabolically active organs in the body, consuming roughly 20 percent of total energy despite accounting for only 2 percent of body weight. This intense activity generates oxidative stress, making the brain particularly vulnerable to damage from insufficient antioxidant protection.

Previous research has established that vitamin C concentrations in the brain are 10 to 15 times higher than in blood plasma, suggesting the organ actively hoards the nutrient. The Hirosaki study is among the first to link plasma levels directly to structural brain differences visible on MRI.

The Limits

This is an observational study, and Shintaku is careful to note that it does not prove cause and effect. People with lower vitamin C levels may differ from those with higher levels in ways the researchers couldn't fully measure — dietary patterns, socioeconomic status, or underlying health conditions that both reduce vitamin C intake and independently affect brain health.

"Larger, more diverse studies are needed to confirm these findings," the authors wrote.

Randomised controlled trials of vitamin C supplementation and cognitive outcomes have produced mixed results, partly because most have been conducted in populations that already consumed adequate amounts. The benefit, if real, may be most pronounced in people who are deficient or borderline.

The South Asian Angle

Here's where the diaspora story gets interesting. Traditional Indian diets are among the richest natural sources of vitamin C in the world. Amla alone contains between 600 and 1,800 milligrams per 100 grams, depending on the variety — compared to about 53 milligrams in an orange. Guava, another subcontinental staple, delivers roughly 228 milligrams per fruit.

Fresh green chutneys made with coriander and mint, raw mango preparations, lemon-dressed salads, and tomato-based gravies all contribute significant vitamin C to a traditional Indian plate. Even the humble nimbu paani — fresh lime water — delivers more of the nutrient than most Western fruit juices.

But the advantage is fragile. Vitamin C is heat-sensitive and water-soluble, meaning it degrades during prolonged cooking and leaches into discarded cooking water. As diaspora families shift toward reheated meals, canned vegetables, and supplements over fresh produce, the natural dietary edge can erode.

The implications are particularly relevant for ageing NRIs. India's traditional dietary patterns, when maintained, may offer a form of neuroprotection that no supplement can fully replicate — because whole foods deliver vitamin C alongside fibre, polyphenols, and other compounds that work synergistically.

Practical Steps

The recommended daily intake of vitamin C is 75 milligrams for women and 90 milligrams for men, though many nutrition scientists argue these targets are set too low. Getting enough from food is straightforward if you eat fresh produce daily:

  • One medium guava provides about 228 mg
  • A tablespoon of amla powder delivers roughly 100 mg
  • One large bell pepper contains about 150 mg
  • A cup of fresh strawberries provides about 85 mg
  • One orange provides about 70 mg

The key is consistency and freshness. Vitamin C cannot be stored in the body for long; it needs to be replenished daily. And the Hirosaki data suggests that what matters for the brain may not be occasional megadoses but steady, sustained levels over years and decades.

The Bigger Picture

This study arrives alongside a growing body of research suggesting that cognitive decline is not an inevitable part of ageing. A parallel study from the Center for BrainHealth at the University of Texas, published in Frontiers in Psychology, found that proactive brain training — structured cognitive exercises done before problems emerge — can measurably improve mental wellness in adults of all ages.

The emerging picture is one of agency: what you eat, how you train your mind, and whether you maintain protective habits over decades all shape the trajectory of brain ageing. For a diaspora that has inherited one of the world's richest culinary traditions, the question is whether that inheritance will be preserved or quietly replaced by convenience.

The study was published in PLOS ONE on June 10, 2026.
